snippet.title: Michael Jackson's costume designer on late singer's iconic outfits
snippet.description:
(6 Aug 2012) 'MICHAEL WOULD SING THE BEAT AND THE CLOTHES HAD TO SHOW YOU THE BEAT'
The zipper-covered "Beat It" jacket. The military-inspired coats with their epaulets, crests and insignias. And, of course, that glittery glove. 
Michael Jackson's fashion sense was as singular as his musical style and dance moves. Millions imitated his pegged pants and penny loafers, a fedora cocked just so. 
Jackson's longtime costumer Michael Bush reveals the secrets behind the King of Pop's meticulously crafted, regal rock-star look-and an intimate glimpse into the man himself-in a colorful new book, "The King of Style: Dressing Michael Jackson." 
"Michael was very hands-on when it came to working with his costumes," said Bush. "He was very there like on a daily, hourly basis with it. And it was like Michael's concept was I want the fashion designers in the world, the big conglomerates, I want them to copy me. I don't want to wear basically what's out there. I want to push my individuality and being that my music's me, my look should be me. And it was always going out studying to see what's out in the world and Michael's concept was we study what's out there, now we have to top it. What's the next look? Where's it going to go next?"
Jackson's stage costumes were designed to display his dance moves, so Bush and his partner Dennis Tompkins, who died last December, were treated to regular private dance recitals to inform their work. 
"Michael would sing the beat and the clothes had to show you the beat," said Bush. "So the clothes had to really extend his, the way he danced, his dance style, so that's why everything was pretty form-fitting because of his locking, popping type style of dancing. If you had these baggy clothes on, like for instance what the rappers are wearing, like Mark would say I'd be in here working my hind end off and you couldn't see anything besides all this fabric. I need you to see the art of the dance. So that's why the clothes were very, very  form-fitting."
Bush and Tompkins worked with Jackson until the pop star's death in June 2009. Though they weren't in charge of the costumes for the ill-fated "This Is It" comeback tour, Jackson's longtime costume designers created ensembles for seven songs, including a reprise of his "Billie Jean" outfit with its loafers and spangled socks. There was also a burgundy and gold monogrammed top with a Chinese collar and bell sleeves, and a pair of black bedazzled shin guards. 
Bush declined to share any details about Jackson's health or demeanor in his final days. He did say, though, that the King of Pop had always hoped his costumes would be celebrated in books and museums, and Bush is humbled by making that dream a reality. The costumer will exhibit some of Jackson's performance outfits in South America, Europe and Asia before releasing his book on Oct. 30. Many of the costumes will be sold at auction in December, with a portion of the proceeds benefiting the Recording Academy's MusiCares charity.

The details on Michael Jackson’s jacket… ✨

I had the chance to see this incredible black-and-gold jacket up close in London, and the craftsmanship is even more impressive in person.

Created by longtime costume designers Dennis Tompkins and Michael Bush, the jacket features 18-karat gold bullion braid and 84 gold-coloured buttons, with intricate military-inspired detailing throughout.

Dating from the 1994–1996 period, the jacket is associated with Michael’s Dangerous and HIStory eras, including his appearance at the Elvis: The Tribute concert and the HIStory World Tour.

Seeing the buttons, sleeves and gold detailing up close was something else. 🖤✨

snippet.title: Michael Jackson  Favourite Costume for his Last Trip by Michael Bush English subtitles
snippet.description:
Michael Jackson Favourite Costume for his Last Trip by Michael Bush English subtitles
Michael Bush's tell-all fashion book about singer Michael Jackson has been in the works for two decades. But Bush's closely guarded secrets as the king of pop's personal dresser and designer aren't tabloid fodder. They're fascinating insider tidbits about his superstar client and friend.
For instance, Jackson only danced in Florsheim loafers, and he instructed Bush to never, under any circumstances, polish them.

So his fans in the back row could see him moonwalk, Jackson danced in white socks covered with nearly 5,000 rhinestones (each hand sewn) and high-water pants — or “floods” as Jackson called them. Military-inspired jackets became his trademark because the style was worn by royalty during Victorian times as a form of entertainment.
When Jackson died on June 25, 2009, La Toya Jackson phoned Bush and told him, “The family wants you to design and make Michael's burial outfit.”

“I told La Toya, 'I don't think I can do that,'” Bush recalled.

But La Toya was insistent.

“'You have to,'” she told me. “'Who else would do it?' She was right. Who else would do it?”

Jackson's garments, which took Bush and Tompkins five days to complete (Bush spent an hour putting them on Jackson, saying his own personal goodbye), were anything but mournful. They were sumptuous: a milky white military jacket saturated with pearls and cream-colored glass bugle beads, and black leather pants adorned with black seed beads. Cherubs held a crown on a gold bejeweled oversized belt. A British royal crest decorated an armband. And Tinker Bell was slinging glittered dust inside the right breast of his jacket; the fairy was Jackson's ultimate fantasy character “because he would say when she slings her dust, the magic begins.”

“I asked La Toya what shoes should he wear because when he wasn't performing, he wore Beatle boots,” Bush said. “La Toya told me: 'Bush, he has to go out of this world dancing. Definitely the Florsheims.'”

snippet.description:
Μichael Jackson's Red Bracelet English subtitles

Everyone was always asking about the red bracelet Michael Jackson wore around his wrist. It was a friendship bracelet that was given to him, and he was told he had to wear it until it fell off. He wanted to have a bracelet like it made to give to the crew of the This Is It tour to solidify the unity in the project and to remind us to heal the world.
(2009), Michaels make-up/hair artist and dear friend of mine, Karen Faye came to me and asked if I would be interested in doing it. Another essential part of his style was the single sequined glove, originally designed by Bill Whitten, who understood MJ’s obsession with sparkle and movement. The glove was carefully encrusted with rhinestones that caught the stage lights perfectly when he performed the moonwalk. Whitten also created many of Michael’s crystal-covered socks, shimmering shirts, and unforgettable “Billie Jean” outfits.

Michael’s Thriller jacket, designed by Deborah Nadoolman Landis, became a pop culture icon on its own red leather, angular shoulders, and black V-shaped detailing that gave him a supernatural, cinematic look. For “Bad,” fashion legend Michael Bush crafted a rebellious biker aesthetic with buckles, straps, metal hardware, and tight leather that highlighted Michael’s edgy transformation. During the Dangerous World Tour, he wore the gold metallic armor-like outfit designed by Bush and Tompkins, inspired by space-age warriors, engineered from flexible materials so he could dance freely while looking futuristic and invincible. Even the simplest outfits, like his white shirts and black trousers for performances like “Smooth Criminal” or “Black or White,” were meticulously tailored flowing fabric designed to float dramatically with every spin, kick, and lean. Stage lighting was planned with the costumes so the shine, shimmer, and shadows would amplify his moves.

Every costume Michael wore was built around his philosophy: clothes should enhance magic. Whether the Swarovski-crystal jackets, military uniforms, fedora hats, loafers with special textured soles for smooth gliding, or his iconic armband symbols, his designers especially Bill Whitten, Michael Bush, and Dennis Tompkins made sure each outfit was more than fashion. snippet.title: Why Did Michael Jackson Tape His Fingers and Wear Masks?
snippet.description:
🧤 Two of the most recognizable visual signatures in entertainment history — white tape wrapped around the fingertips and surgical masks covering the face — belonged to a single man. For decades, the public assumed they knew why. The tape was a fashion quirk. The masks were germaphobia. The glove was vanity. Every explanation the media offered was wrong.
In this video, we pull apart each of Michael Jackson's signature visual elements and reveal the actual, documented reasons behind them — straight from Michael's own mouth and from the people who worked closest to him:
The Taped Fingers:
▪️ Musical director Michael Bearden asked Michael directly: "MJ, why you have tape on your hands?"
▪️ Michael's answer: "Well, 'cause it feels good. It was like a batter in a batter's box"

snippet.title: How to do: Create a Michael Jackson Costume For Halloween
snippet.description:
Be the King of Pop on Halloween with any one of these iconic looks.

 Instructions   Quick Tip: 

 Get a few friends to dress in an identical manner as your back-up singers. Step 1 Keep it simple with the look Michael wore to the 1995 MTV Video Music Awards: All you need is a black suit jacket with a thick white armband wrapped around your bicep, matching black pants that end just above the ankle, a white dress shirt, a skinny black tie, white dress socks, and black penny loafers. 

 Step 2 Mimic Michael's 'Bad' look: Start with a black or vinyl motorcycle jacket and sew two black buckles over one shoulder, as well as around the cuffs, above the elbows, and around the collar. Team with skintight black jeans and black buckled shoes. 

 Step 3 To represent Michael Jackson circa 2004, wear a white suit jacket with a gold armband; a white dress shirt with gold buttons, buttoned to your neck; white dress pants, and white shoes. Ask a (preferably burly) friend to go as your bodyguard: All they have to do is wear a black suit with a white shirt, and hold a black umbrella over you.  Did You Know: 

 Michael Jackson's famous white gloves were made of spandex and covered with clear loch rosen Swarovski crystals that were hand-sewn on with white thread. Step 4 Be a 'Smooth Criminal': Wear a light-colored pin-striped suit with matching tie, a dark shirt, suspenders, dress shoes, an armband, and a fedora. 

 Step 5 Look like Michael did when he debuted the moonwalk in 1983: A blue sequined shirt, black sequined jacket, cropped blank pants, sparkly white socks, black penny loafers, and a white glove.  Quick Tip: 

 All of Michael Jackson's stage pants ended above the ankle so the audience could see his fancy footwork. Step 6 Beat everyone else's costume with an outfit inspired by Michael's 1982 video, 'Beat It': Top a blue, pink, and gray t-shirt with a red leather or vinyl jacket. Glue 5-inch zippers on the front and sleeves of the jacket, and sew gold lame diamond-shaped patches just below the shoulders on each side. Wear the sleeves pushed up to your elbows. 

 Step 7 Mimic Michael's military look: Cover a cropped, double-breasted jacket with blue sequins, and add gold epaulets, gold embroidery on the sleeves, and a gold sash. Wear with navy blue dress pants, a white tuxedo shirt, a white sequined glove, and oversized aviator sunglasses. 

 Step 8 Tell everyone that 'Billie Jean' is not your lover while wearing a black leather or vinyl suit with a pale pink dress shirt, red bow tie, pale pink dress socks, and white shoes. 

 Step 9 Thrill everyone with Michael's 'Thriller' look: Take a red leather or vinyl jacket, sew in shoulder pads, and use black duct tape to line the waistband and to make an angled stripe on each side to form a V. Team with tight red jeans or pants, white socks, and black penny loafers.

snippet.title: The Watch the Army Refused to Issue — So Soldiers Bought Seikos Themselves in Vietnam
snippet.description:
Turn over an American issue watch from Vietnam and read the back. Wrist watch, non-maintainable. A stock number. A date. Nobody planned to fix it. When it stopped, it was finished.

In 1964 the United States wrote the rules for the watch its soldiers would wear into war, and the rules said it could be thrown away. Plastic case. Lower accuracy. And no hacking, the one feature that let a whole unit start their second hands on the same word.

The version most people know is simple. The Army was cheap, the soldiers were smart, they bought Seikos. The documents tell it in a stranger order. Many men were never issued a watch at all, and the store they bought the better one from was the Army's own PX. A sailor at Subic Bay paid under a hundred dollars for his first Seiko. A Rolex Submariner in the same stores ran about 190 to 240.

And one secret office had already made the same choice. The recon teams of MACV-SOG, sent into Laos and Cambodia where Americans were not supposed to be, asked their supply office on Okinawa for a dozen or so Rolex Oysters. According to the deputy director's own account, they got Seiko watches instead, at six or eight dollars apiece. The institution knew the Japanese watch was good enough for its most dangerous missions. It bought them. It issued them. It just did not issue them to everyone else.

What we go through:

The 1964 disposable spec, MIL-W-46374, and the hand-wound hacking watch it replaced Why a supply officer with half a million troops to equip thought it made sense Elgin and Hamilton, the Swiss cartel complaint, and the end of American watchmaking Seiko's first dive watch, the 6105, and war money flowing into Japanese industry Mickey Mouse watches, and what the evidence does and does not show CISO, sterile gear, and the Seikos issued to SOG Deniability or budget John Stryker Meyer's tritium dial and the midnight radio checks Michael O'Byrne, a Seiko, a compass on the strap, and a grenade The Senate club and PX corruption hearings The Benrus Type I and Type II, sixteen thousand made and none sold to the public Quartz, the spec that outlived its industry, and Apocalypse Now The G-Shock in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the thousand SOCOM bought in 2014

Said plainly on the evidence: the stories of issued watches leaking and failing come from later histories and watch writing. No field report or letter home saying it has surfaced. What survived is the buying. And nothing in the Senate hearings ties the PX scandal to watches.

There is no villain in this. Nobody planned the loop. It happened anyway, and then popular memory kept the Seiko and quietly lost the specification.

Next time you see a black-dial watch on an old veteran's wrist, ask him where he got it.

Tell me in the comments: did you, or someone in your family, ever buy your own watch in uniform, and what was it?
